SceneDiff Benchmark is potentially valuable: it contains 350 real-world video pairs, 1009 changed objects, dense masks across visible frames, varied indoor/outdoor scenes, an egocentric kitchen subset, change-type labels, and both per-view and per-scene evaluation.

The method is technically coherent and training-free. Joint feed-forward reconstruction, co-visible frame pairing, asymmetric depth reasoning, reprojected DINO features, SAM regions, and cross-frame instance association form a sensible pipeline for suppressing viewpoint-induced false changes.

Results are consistently strong: SceneDiff substantially exceeds the evaluated baselines on both benchmark subsets, improves RC-3D AP50, and also performs competitively on ChangeSim. Ablations identify the importance of the geometry backbone and appearance-reprojection cue, while threshold sensitivity, runtime, qualitative failures, and a robotic demonstration provide useful supporting evidence.

The manuscript is clear and visually polished. It explains the task, metric, method, annotation workflow, baseline adaptations, runtime, and limitations in considerable detail; the discussion of ambiguity, repeated objects, lighting variation, and reconstruction failure is appropriately candid.
weaknesses: The benchmark comparison is not yet sufficiently comprehensive. Several relevant recent methods discussed in related work—such as zero-shot object-level change detection, visual-correspondence approaches, foundation-model/cross-attention methods, and ViewDelta—are not evaluated. On the new benchmark, the principal comparisons are CYWS-3D, a weak VLM-plus-grounding pipeline, and heavily adapted 3DGS-CD; only SceneDiff reports all per-scene metrics. Thus the large relative gains do not by themselves establish superiority over the strongest adaptable alternatives or simpler geometry-plus-feature baselines.

The proposed metric is unusually permissive and only weakly measures localization. Masks or boxes are reduced to centroid points, a prediction is correct whenever its point lies inside a ground-truth bounding box, and up to two detections per object are allowed without penalty. This can conceal poor mask boundaries, coarse localization, over-segmentation, and duplicate predictions, despite the method claiming object masks. Standard mask/box AP and results without the duplicate tolerance are needed.

The split construction is insufficiently documented. The 350 pairs come from only 50 scenes, and the collection instructions explicitly encourage recording multiple versions to create more pairs, yet the paper says only that video pairs—not physical scenes—are divided into validation and test sets. Without an explicit scene-disjoint split, validation/test leakage and inflated generalization estimates are plausible, especially because thresholds and other hyperparameters are selected on validation data.

Important ablations are reported on the SD-V test set rather than validation, weakening experimental hygiene. There is also no component analysis of frame pairing, 3D score aggregation, cross-frame association, or change-type matching, and no comparison against independently reconstructing then registering the two captures. Consequently, the evidence does not fully isolate the claimed benefits of joint geometry and object association.

Dataset quality and reproducibility documentation need strengthening. The paper gives no inter-annotator agreement, independent mask audit, annotation error rate, annotator count, or detailed breakdown of collection sources. Exact pretrained model variants and several implementation choices are also under-specified. The promise to release derived HD-Epic data “for any use” should be reconciled with source licenses, consent, and privacy requirements.

Absolute performance remains modest on the harder setting: SD-K reaches 23.6 per-view AP, 20.9 per-scene AP, and 12.2 type-aware AP. Dynamic people must be manually masked, and limited overlap, repeated instances, strong illumination changes, and reconstruction failures remain serious limitations. These are acknowledged, but they constrain immediate reliability in the motivating robotics and monitoring applications.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored computer-vision problem: instance-level object change detection across videos captured from substantially different viewpoints.

The SceneDiff benchmark is potentially valuable. It contains 350 real-world video pairs, 1,009 annotated changed objects, dense masks across visible frames, two distinct data subsets, and both per-view and per-scene evaluation.

The training-free pipeline is coherent: joint 3D reconstruction, co-visible view selection, geometry and DINO feature comparison, SAM regions, and cross-frame instance association form a sensible system. It substantially outperforms the evaluated baselines, including 46.3 per-scene AP on SD-V and 68.7 AP50 on RC-3D.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. The supplement reports runtime, threshold sensitivity, reconstruction-backbone comparisons, challenging cases, and honest limitations involving repetitive objects, lighting, reconstruction failures, and dynamic content.
weaknesses: The dataset split is a major concern. The 350 pairs come from only 50 scenes, but the paper describes validation and test splits in terms of video pairs without stating that physical scenes are disjoint. If captures of the same scene occur in both splits, validation-based tuning can leak scene appearance and geometry into the test evaluation. Scene-disjoint splits and explicit split statistics are necessary.

The proposed evaluation is unusually permissive. Predicted masks are reduced to centroid points, ground-truth masks to bounding boxes, and two detections per object are allowed without penalty. This discards segmentation quality and may reward coarse or duplicated predictions. The special CYWS-3D protocol additionally ignores some otherwise false-positive source-view predictions when their paired prediction matches ground truth, further complicating interpretation.

Evidence against prior work is limited. On SceneDiff, the comparison comprises a weak VLM pipeline, a 3DGS method operating far outside favorable capture conditions, and CYWS-3D, which cannot perform the principal per-scene task. The authors also alter 3DGS-CD by removing its occupancy-grid stage. Missing are simple component-matched baselines using the same geometry, SAM, and DINO features, as well as comparisons to more of the recent methods discussed in related work. Consequently, the headline relative improvement is less convincing than it appears.

Table 4 explicitly performs extensive ablations on the SD-V test set rather than the validation set, creating a risk that the held-out test set influenced design conclusions. The ablations also omit the substantially harder SD-K subset.

Dataset reliability is insufficiently documented. There is no inter-annotator agreement, independent audit, quantitative mask-quality assessment, or detailed breakdown of scenes and sources across splits. The claim of “thousands of changed objects” also conflicts with the reported total of 1,009. Release rights and redistribution conditions for the HD-Epic-derived portion are not discussed despite the promise to release the dataset “for any use.”

The algorithmic novelty is modest, consisting primarily of combining pretrained π3, DINO, and SAM models with hand-designed reprojection scores and heuristic association. Several weights and thresholds are introduced, but sensitivity is shown only for the change and merging thresholds; calibration of cue weights, visibility rules, and moved-object similarity is not adequately justified.

Practical claims are stronger than the evidence. Performance remains low on SD-K (20.9 per-scene AP and 12.2 APtype), dynamic people require manually supplied masks, inference averages 159.4 seconds per pair on an A40, and the robot application is a single controlled qualitative demonstration without success rates or comparison baselines.

Overall, the benchmark could become useful, but the potentially non-scene-disjoint evaluation, permissive metric, and weak baseline suite prevent the current empirical results from establishing a sufficiently reliable scientific case for acceptance. These are substantive issues rather than presentation-level corrections.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, this is best assessed primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with an accompanying algorithm. SceneDiff fills a meaningful gap: multiview, instance-level change detection across different camera trajectories. Its 350 video pairs, 1,009 changed objects, dense visible-frame masks, change-type labels, and per-view/per-scene protocols constitute a useful computer-vision benchmark.

The training-free method is technically coherent. Joint 3D reconstruction, co-visibility-based frame pairing, asymmetric depth reasoning, DINO appearance comparison, SAM regions, and cross-view instance association form a sensible pipeline for suppressing viewpoint-induced false changes.

The empirical gains are substantial: per-view AP reaches 49.6 versus 26.9 on SD-V and 23.6 versus 10.8 on the harder SD-K subset; RC-3D AP50 improves from 50.0 to 68.7. Results on ChangeSim further suggest applicability beyond the new benchmark.

The evidence is broad and unusually informative: cue/backbone ablations, threshold sensitivity, multiple geometry models, two benchmark subsets, RC-3D and ChangeSim transfer, runtime reporting, qualitative comparisons, stress tests, failure analysis, and a robotic tidying demonstration.

The manuscript is clear and visually effective. It defines the task and evaluation carefully, provides many implementation parameters, describes the annotation workflow, and candidly discusses ambiguity, reconstruction failures, repetitive clutter, lighting changes, and low-overlap views.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is quite permissive: predictions are reduced to centroid points, any point inside a ground-truth bounding box counts, and up to two detections per object incur no penalty. This discards the quality of the densely annotated masks, can favor large objects, and may inflate AP through duplicate predictions. Standard box/mask AP or sensitivity analyses for these choices would make the benchmark more convincing.

Baseline coverage is limited relative to the related work. Several recent zero-shot, correspondence-based, and text-conditioned change-detection methods cited in the paper are not evaluated. The strongest multiview baselines also perform extremely poorly, and 3DGS-CD and CYWS-3D are materially adapted for this evaluation, making the size of the claimed state-of-the-art margin harder to interpret.

Change-type classification remains weak: APtype is only 25.5 on SD-V and 12.2 on SD-K, versus type-agnostic per-scene AP of 46.3 and 20.9. The simple rule that feature-similar detections across videos are 'Moved' is vulnerable to repeated objects, yet the paper does not provide per-type AP, confusion matrices, or a detailed quantitative diagnosis.

The benchmark split construction is underspecified. The paper does not clearly state whether validation and test sets are disjoint by physical scene, capture session, or HD-Epic source video. With 200 pairs drawn from only 50 manually collected scenes, scene-level separation is important even for a training-free paper and essential for future learned methods.

Dataset validation is not quantified beyond the annotation workflow and review interface: inter-annotator agreement, audit error rates, and treatment of ambiguous object identity or granularity are absent. The promised 'any use' release should also clarify redistribution and licensing constraints for the HD-Epic-derived subset.

The method is computationally heavy at about 159 seconds per sequence pair, depends strongly on multiple large pretrained components, and fails when geometry reconstruction or overlap is poor. Moreover, most method components are established techniques; the algorithmic originality lies mainly in their thoughtful integration, so the benchmark is the stronger contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: identifying added, removed, and moved object instances across videos captured at different times and along different camera trajectories.

The SceneDiff benchmark is a substantial contribution. It contains 350 real-world video pairs, 1,009 changed objects, indoor and outdoor environments, and consistent cross-view instance masks. The proposed per-scene object AP usefully evaluates whether a method consistently identifies physical objects rather than producing disconnected frame-level detections.

The training-free method is technically well motivated: joint geometry estimation establishes a common frame, asymmetric depth reasoning helps handle occlusion, DINO features provide appearance cues, and SAM regions convert noisy pixel evidence into object-level predictions and tracks.

Experimental results are broad and generally compelling. SceneDiff substantially improves the reported per-image and per-scene results on the new benchmark, improves AP50 on the independent RC-3D benchmark from 50.0 to 65.3 over the strongest sensor-depth baseline, and remains competitive on PASLCD and ChangeSim despite those datasets targeting somewhat different settings.

The ablations examine geometry backbones, feature backbones, and combinations of the three scoring cues. The supplement additionally provides threshold sensitivity, runtime, challenging cases, and analyses of reconstruction failure, lighting variation, repetitive objects, and large amounts of scene change.

The manuscript is clear and visually effective, and it candidly reports low absolute scene-level AP, inherent ambiguity between identical instances, reliance on geometry estimation, and other concrete failure modes.
weaknesses: The comparison on the new benchmark is not fully controlled. Baselines have different native outputs, are converted using SAM, and receive method-specific adaptations. In particular, CYWS-3D is supplied with SceneDiff's π3 depth and uses a rule that can discard a source-view false positive when its paired prediction matches ground truth; 3DGS-CD is evaluated without its occupancy-grid stage. These choices are explained but make the headline relative improvements difficult to interpret as direct method-to-method comparisons.

Evidence for the benchmark's annotation reliability is incomplete. The paper describes the SAM2-assisted workflow and manual review, but reports no independent annotation audit, inter-annotator agreement, mask-quality measurement, or analysis of missed changed objects. This matters because the principal contribution depends on dense and cross-view-consistent instance labels.

Dataset diversity is more limited than the pair count suggests: the 350 pairs come from only 50 physical scenes, the manually collected subset involved seven collectors, and multiple pairs can originate from the same scene. Scene-level splitting prevents direct leakage, but the paper should report scenes, videos, and pairs per split and clarify how pairs were constructed so that the effective sample size is transparent.

The method's absolute performance remains modest on its central metric: obj/sc AP is 22.8 on SD-V and 10.6 on SD-K. This supports the value of the benchmark, but limits claims that the approach already provides reliable object inventories for applications such as warehousing, disaster response, or robotic tidying.

The robot demonstration is qualitative and does not substantiate the claimed practical utility: there are no repeated trials, task-success rates, comparisons, or analysis separating perception errors from manipulation performance.

Several methodological details are ambiguous. The prose describes using only non-negative depth differences, whereas the visibility mask permits values down to -0.02, and Eq. 4 appears to average the raw geometry score without explicitly masking invalid reprojections. The direction of the 'more than 50% pixels masked' condition is also unclear. These issues should be resolved in the specification or released implementation.

The claim that SceneDiff 'naturally improves as the underlying models advance' is stronger than the evidence. The feature ablation is not monotonic across DINO generations for all metrics, and the tested geometry models do not establish that chronological backbone improvement reliably translates into better change detection.

Results lack uncertainty estimates or robustness across alternative scene splits. Given only 50 physical scenes and substantial category variation, bootstrap confidence intervals or per-scene distributions would make the reported margins more convincing.

Reproducibility and responsible release details remain incomplete: code and data are promised rather than available in the manuscript, and the paper does not clearly document dataset licensing, participant consent/release procedures, privacy auditing, or the redistribution terms for the HD-Epic-derived subset.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best assessed primarily as Datasets/Benchmarks, with the algorithm as a secondary contribution. The proposed method is technically coherent: joint geometry estimation establishes a common frame, asymmetric depth reasoning handles visibility, DINO features provide appearance evidence, SAM regions suppress pixel-level noise, and multiview association produces scene-level object hypotheses.

Results are broad and consistently favorable. SceneDiff substantially improves the reported object/image and object/scene AP on the new test set, reaches 65.3 AP50 on RC-3D versus 50.0 for the strongest reported sensor-depth baseline, and remains competitive on PASLCD and ChangeSim.

The paper includes useful ablations over geometry backbones, feature backbones, individual cues, and hyperparameters, as well as runtime measurements and informative failure analyses involving repetitive objects, limited overlap, lighting changes, and large-scale scene modification.

The manuscript is clear and visually polished. The task, metrics, pipeline, annotation interface, baseline adaptations, and collection instructions are described in substantial detail, and code, evaluation tools, and data are promised for release.
weaknesses: The strongest evidence comes from the authors' own benchmark, while the scene-level comparison there is weak: obj/sc AP is compared only against an adapted 3DGS method and a VLM pipeline, both of which perform near the floor. A stronger multiview object-mapping or segmentation-and-tracking baseline is needed to establish that the association component, rather than the pretrained foundation-model stack, drives the gain.

The primary obj/sc AP is change-type agnostic even though predicting Added, Removed, or Moved is part of the stated task. The stricter type-aware results appear only in the supplement and fall from 22.8 to 18.5 on SD-V and from 10.6 to 7.7 on SD-K. Type-aware evaluation should be primary and broken down by change type.

Dataset validation is insufficiently documented for a benchmark contribution. The paper reports annotation time and a review interface, but no inter-annotator agreement, independent quality audit, mask-error estimate, or adjudication protocol. It also does not clearly report the prevalence and handling of zero-change pairs, which are important for measuring false alarms in deployment.

The benchmark contains only 50 physical scenes, with the manually collected portion gathered by seven people under instructions that avoid dynamic objects, motion blur, identity information, substantially dissimilar coverage, and other difficult conditions. Scene-wise splitting is appropriate, but confidence intervals or variability across scenes are absent, and the controlled collection limits support for broad real-world generalization claims.

The method is mostly a carefully engineered composition of π3, DINO, and SAM with several heuristic thresholds and greedy association steps. Its algorithmic originality is moderate, and performance remains low on the central scene-level task, especially on SD-K (10.6 AP; 7.7 when type-aware). Moreover, removing the geometry cue improves obj/sc AP by 2.6 points in the ablation, so the full configuration is not optimal for the metric the paper calls most important.

Baseline evaluation involves substantial method-specific adaptation, including view pairing, SAM conversion, supplied π3 depth or poses, and special false-positive handling for CYWS-3D. These choices are explained, but they make the comparison harder to interpret and should be complemented by standardized input/output conditions and results without bespoke post-processing.

The robotic tidying application is anecdotal: it uses an extra RealSense frame for alignment and reports no number of trials, success rate, baseline, recovery behavior, or safety analysis. It illustrates feasibility but does not substantiate the paper's practical-utility claim.

strengths: This is best assessed as a mixed Datasets/Benchmarks and Algorithms contribution. The benchmark is arguably the stronger contribution: it introduces a useful multiview setting with different camera trajectories, 350 real-world video pairs, 1,009 changed objects, dense cross-view instance annotations, and both indoor and outdoor scenes.

The proposed scene-level object metric addresses an important limitation of per-frame evaluation by testing whether a system consistently identifies the same physical object across views. The accompanying per-pixel and per-image metrics retain comparability with prior work.

SceneDiff is a sensible and technically coherent training-free pipeline. Joint geometric reconstruction, co-visibility-based frame pairing, asymmetric depth reasoning, DINO appearance comparison, SAM regions, and cross-frame instance association directly address viewpoint variation and occlusion.

The empirical results are consistently strong. SceneDiff substantially outperforms adapted baselines on both SceneDiff subsets, improves RC-3D AP50 from 50.0 to 65.3, and remains competitive or superior on PASLCD and ChangeSim, providing useful evidence beyond the authors' own benchmark.

The ablations are informative: they isolate the geometric, reprojected-feature, and region-matching cues; compare multiple geometry and DINO backbones; and show that accurate geometry is particularly important. The supplement also includes parameter sensitivity, runtime, change-type-aware evaluation, and concrete failure analyses.

The paper is clear and visually effective, provides implementation parameters, describes baseline adaptations in detail, and states that code, data, annotation tooling, and evaluation code will be released. The robotic tidying demonstration further illustrates practical utility.
weaknesses: The main obj/sc AP is change-type agnostic, although predicting Added, Removed, or Moved is central to the task definition and claimed output. The stricter type-aware results are only supplementary and fall from 22.8 to 18.5 on SD-V and from 10.6 to 7.7 on SD-K. Type-aware evaluation should be a primary metric, with per-class AP or a confusion analysis.

Benchmark annotation quality is insufficiently quantified. The paper describes SAM2 propagation and manual review, but reports no independent double annotation, inter-annotator agreement, mask-quality audit, or error rate. Such validation is important for a benchmark intended to support fine-grained instance and track evaluation.

The dataset contains only 50 physical scenes, despite 350 sequence pairs. Because pairs from a scene are correlated, aggregate AP over pairs may overstate the effective diversity and certainty of the comparison. Per-scene variability, confidence intervals, or bootstrap significance tests would strengthen the evidence.

Several baselines require substantial author-designed adaptations: shared regressed poses, SAM conversion, an empirical 60% threshold for MV3DCD, omission of 3DGS-CD's occupancy-grid stage, and manual matching of VLM text outputs to ground-truth labels. These choices are discussed but make the headline comparison less clean; additional independently reproducible or native multiview baselines would improve confidence.

Algorithmic novelty is moderate because the method primarily composes pretrained π3, DINOv3, and SAM components with heuristic thresholds and ConceptGraph-style association. Its value lies more in the formulation, benchmark, and effective integration than in a fundamentally new learning or geometric technique.

Absolute performance remains limited on the principal scene-level task: 22.8 obj/sc AP on SD-V and 10.6 on SD-K. Runtime is also substantial at 159.4 seconds per sequence pair, and scaling with video length, memory use, and input sampling is not fully characterized. These limitations temper claims of immediate practical deployment but do not outweigh the paper's benchmark and systems contributions.
